defect_description: 'Good morning' is a fixed greeting; 'Хорошее утро' (Good/Nice morning) is a literal word-for-word translation that does not exist as a Russian greeting.
'How are you?' is rendered as 'Как дела?' in Russian; 'Как ты есть?' is a word-for-word translation that sounds foreign and unnatural.
Russian does not use the verb 'есть' (to be) in the present tense predicate; 'Я есть хорошо' is an ungrammatical calque of English.
'Nice to meet you' as a greeting has the fixed Russian equivalent 'Приятно познакомиться'; 'Приятно встретить тебя' (nice to encounter you) is not the standard greeting phrase.
'See you later' is a farewell idiom; the Russian equivalent is 'До встречи' or 'До скорого'; 'Увижу тебя позже' is a literal translation that sounds unnatural as a parting phrase.
'Я нуждаюсь в помощи' is grammatically correct but overly formal and literary; 'Мне нужна помощь' is the natural everyday phrasing.
The Russian for 'What time is it?' is 'Который час?' or 'Сколько времени?'; 'Какое время это есть?' is an ungrammatical literal translation.
'Извините' is the correct imperative form used as an apology; 'Извиняй меня' uses the wrong aspect and form of the verb.
'Я не понимаю' uses the correct first-person indicative; 'понимай' is an imperative form and ungrammatical in this context.
The polite imperative is 'Повторите'; 'повторяйте' is an imperfective form that implies repeated action, which is incorrect here.
'помедленнее' is the natural comparative adverb; 'более медленно' is a formal analytical comparative that sounds stilted in everyday speech.
'Thank you very much' has the fixed Russian equivalent 'Большое спасибо' or 'Очень вам благодарен'; 'Спасибо очень много' is a word-for-word literal translation that does not work in Russian.
'You're welcome' as a response to thanks is 'Пожалуйста' in Russian; 'Ты приветствован' is a literal translation of 'you are welcomed' which does not serve this function.
'Я сожалею' is a formal expression of regret appropriate for official contexts; 'Прости' or 'Извини' is the natural everyday apology.
'ближайшая' is the superlative meaning 'nearest'; 'ближняя' means simply 'near' or 'close', and adding 'есть' (there is) is an ungrammatical calque.
'Я голоден' is the natural Russian expression for being hungry; 'У меня есть голод' (I have hunger) is a literal calque from English.
'Я хочу пить' (I want to drink) is the natural Russian equivalent; 'Я жаждущий' (I am thirsting) is an overly literary adjective not used in everyday speech.
'На улице' is the Russian idiom for 'outside' or 'outdoors'; 'Снаружи это холодно' uses 'снаружи' (outside of a building) and the unnecessary pronoun 'это'.
'Я устал' is the natural short-form predicative; 'Я являюсь усталым' uses the bookish copula 'являться' and is an unnatural calque of 'I am tired'.
'Good night' is 'Спокойной ночи' (literally 'of a peaceful night'); 'Хорошей ночи' (of a good night) is a literal word-for-word rendering that is not the established Russian farewell.
'I like' is 'Мне нравится'; 'Я люблю' means 'I love', which is a stronger feeling and changes the meaning.
'Weather' is 'погода' in Russian; 'метеорология' means meteorology (the science), which is a false cognate error.

source: I'll be back in five minutes.
rejected_translation: Я буду обратно в пять минут.
defect_description: 'Я вернусь через пять минут' is the natural Russian; 'буду обратно в пять минут' is a literal translation of English word order that sounds unnatural in Russian.
'помогать' is the imperfective meaning ongoing help; 'помочь' (perfective) is correct for a one-time offer of assistance. 'Могу я' is also an unusual word order.
In Russian 'говорить по-русски' (speak in Russian) requires the prepositional prefix 'по-'; 'говорить русский' (speak Russian) treats language as a direct object incorrectly.
'ощущаю' and 'великолепно' are elevated, literary words; 'чувствую себя отлично' is the natural everyday expression.
'Я забыл ключи' is the standard everyday expression; 'позабыл о своих ключах' is more literary and implies forgetting entirely, which changes the nuance.
'I'm running late' means опаздываю (I am late); 'Я бегу поздно' (I'm running late) is a literal word-for-word translation with the physical meaning of running.
'Watch out' is an idiom meaning be careful; 'Наблюдай снаружи' (watch outside) is a nonsensical literal translation.
'Не проблема' is the natural colloquial equivalent; 'Никакой проблемы нет' is a more formal, verbose version not typical of casual speech.
'убеждён' means convinced, not uncertain; 'Я не убеждён' means 'I am not convinced', which has a different nuance from simple uncertainty.
'интересующее' is a participial form (the thing that is causing interest); 'интересно' is the short-form adjective used as a predicate, which is correct here.
'Я согласен' uses the correct short-form adjective; 'Я соглашаю' attempts to use 'соглашать' as a transitive verb without an object, which is ungrammatical in this construction.
'Дайте думать' or 'Дай подумаю' are natural Russian; 'Дайте мне думать' (let me be thinking) uses the imperfective aspect incorrectly and has unnatural word order.
'I'll do my best' maps to 'Я постараюсь' in Russian; 'Я сделаю моё лучшее' is a word-for-word translation that does not exist as an idiom in Russian.
'Ты отлично выглядишь' is the natural compliment; 'смотришься великолепно' is more literary and less common in everyday compliments.
'Я дома' is the natural conversational phrase; 'Я нахожусь в доме' (I am located inside the house) is overly formal and bureaucratic.
'Я позвоню' (perfective future) is correct for a single future call; 'буду звонить' (imperfective) implies repeated or ongoing calling which is not the intended meaning.
'Take care' as a farewell is 'Береги себя' in Russian; 'Бери уход' is a nonsensical literal translation of the English words.
The rejected translation adds 'человек' (person) which is not in the source and changes the statement from an in-context assertion to a personality description.
'I missed you' (emotionally) is 'Я скучал по тебе'; 'Я пропустил тебя' means I missed you (failed to see/catch you) which is the wrong sense.
'I'm on my way' means I am coming; 'Я нахожусь на своём пути' is a literal translation of 'I am on my path/way' that sounds stilted.
'Неважно' is the natural colloquial equivalent; 'Это не имеет значения' is a formal paraphrase more appropriate for written or official language.

'I need a moment' is 'Мне нужна минута' or 'Дай мне секунду'; 'нуждаюсь в моменте' is a literal translation using a formal register and the English word 'момент' as a false cognate for 'moment' of time.
'What's up?' is an informal greeting equivalent to 'How are you?'; 'Что наверху?' (what is up there/above?) is a nonsensical literal translation.
'проснулся' is the correct reflexive perfective for waking up; 'разбудился' does not exist as a valid reflexive form in standard Russian.
'свободен' is the short-form predicate adjective; 'свободный' is the full form used attributively, not predicatively in this type of sentence.
'Пойдём!' is the natural Russian invitation to go; 'Давай идём!' is understandable but less crisp and not the standard single-word equivalent.
'Я подумаю' uses the perfective future correctly; 'буду думать' (imperfective) implies prolonged thinking and does not convey a promise to consider something.

'Good luck!' is 'Удачи!' in Russian (genitive used as a wish); 'Хорошая удача!' (Good luck!) treats 'good' as an adjective, but Russian expresses this wish with the noun in the genitive without an adjective.
